corrected_value.title_o: The Presence of Variety Reduces Perceived Quantity

decisions.quote:
Redden and Hoch (2009) found that variety in a set of items robustly decreased the
                        perceived quantity of the sum of these items across multiple studies. For example, a set
                        of multicolored M&M’s was estimated to contain fewer M&M’s than an equally large
                        set of single-colored M&M’s (e.g., Redden and Hoch, 2009, Study 3). We conducted
                        six studies with methods that were similar to those used by Redden and Hoch (2009)
                        and did not find this effect in any of them.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding identify Redden and Hoch (2009), 'The presence of variety reduces perceived quantity' (Journal of Consumer Research, 36(3), 406-417, DOI: 10.1086/598971), as the sole published original study re-tested across all six replication studies in this paper. Other cited works provide theoretical background or motivate auxiliary manipulations (such as container shape or anchoring), and internal replications within the paper (Studies 2, 5, and 6 re-testing Studies 1 and 4) are part of the same replication series targeting Redden and Hoch (2009).

decisions.quote:
We conducted
                        six studies with methods that were similar to those used by Redden and Hoch (2009)
                        and did not find this effect in any of them. A meta-analysis of the four original studies
                        and 6 replication studies (N = 1,383) revealed no evidence for the phenomenon that
                        variety reduces perceived quantity.
decisions.reason: Across six high-powered replication studies (three conceptual replications in Studies 1, 2, and 6 and three close replications in Studies 3, 4, and 5; total replication N = 1,077), the authors state an explicit overall failure verdict in the title ('Failures to Replicate Redden and Hoch (2009)'), abstract ('did not find this effect in any of them'), and General Discussion ('In six different studies, we failed to replicate the effect that variety reduces perceived quantity'). Studies 1, 2, and 6 yielded effects in the opposite direction (variety increased perceived quantity) and Studies 3, 4, and 5 yielded null main effects, with a meta-analytic replication effect of d = -0.075 (p = .284) that significantly differed from the original studies (p = .001). Although Study 4 had a stimulus-sampling programming error, the authors note that power was uncompromised and reran the fixed procedure in Study 5 with the same null result, so the overall replication outcome is 'failed'.

decisions.reason: The paper collects new empirical data across six studies with new participant samples (N = 1,077 across Studies 1-6) to re-test the published finding of Redden and Hoch (2009) that variety reduces perceived quantity, making its record type 'replication'.
